alignment.note: Greek παραγγέλλει is present indicative ('he directs/commands'), a vivid historic present typical of Markan narrative; the Vulgate præcepit and Syriac ܘܦܩܕ both render it as a simple past/perfect, levelling the tense. The Syriac verb also carries the prefixed conjunction, so the same token covers both 'and' and 'commanded'.

Greek ἀναπεσεῖν ('to recline') and Latin discumbere reflect the Greco-Roman dining posture; the Syriac ܕܢܣܬܡܟܘܢ (ethpaal of s-m-k, 'to be made to recline/lean') uses an idiomatic Semitic reclining verb and is cast as a finite subordinate clause ('that they should recline') rather than the infinitive of the other two traditions.

Greek λαβών and Latin accipiens are aorist/present participles ('having taken'); the Syriac ܘܢܣܒ is a finite verb carrying the prefixed conjunction, so the single token here corresponds to both 'and' and 'took'.

Greek and Vulgate use the substantival article (τοὺς / no equivalent needed) with 'seven loaves'; the Syriac inserts the independent demonstrative pronoun ܗܢܘܢ ('those') before ܫܒܥܐ ܠܚܡܝܢ, a periphrastic determiner functioning equivalently to the Greek article.

Greek εὐχαριστήσας ('having given thanks') and the Latin periphrasis gratias agens both employ the vocabulary of thanksgiving (eucharistia); the Syriac ܘܒܪܟ (root b-r-k, 'and blessed') substitutes the Semitic idiom of blessing, harmonising with the parallel feeding accounts and the standard Jewish berakhah formula rather than the Greek 'thanksgiving' verb.
Greek ἔκλασεν and Latin fregit render 'he broke'; the Syriac ܘܩܨܐ (q-ṣ-ʾ, 'and broke') carries the prefixed conjunction, so this token also encompasses the connective 'and'.

Greek ἐδίδου is imperfect ('he kept giving'), conveying iterative distribution; the Vulgate dabat preserves this durative aspect, while the Syriac ܘܝܗܒ flattens it to a simple perfect and again absorbs the connective conjunction into the prefixed verb.

Greek and Latin express the possessive analytically (τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ / discipulis suis, 'his disciples'); the Syriac ܠܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ encodes the dative preposition and the third-person possessive suffix synthetically within a single inflected form.

Greek ἵνα παρατιθῶσιν and Latin ut apponerent form a purpose clause with conjunction plus subjunctive; the Syriac ܕܢܣܝܡܘܢ (d- + imperfect of s-y-m) collapses the same final clause into a single prefixed-subordinator verb, semantically equivalent.

Greek παρέθηκαν and Latin apposuerunt use the specific verb 'to set before/serve' (παρατίθημι), repeating the lexeme of the purpose clause; the Syriac ܘܣܡܘ (s-y-m, 'and they placed') uses the general verb 'to set/place' and incorporates the connective, a lexical simplification.
